title: LATTE: Learning Adaptive Segmentation for Efficient and Effective Trajectory Similarity Learning

problem.claim: Trajectory similarity learning models must represent variable-length trajectories as fixed-size vectors while maintaining efficient and effective similarity learning.

gap.claim: Existing map-matching-based TSL models rely on heavy road-network and trajectory modeling structures, causing overfitting and inefficiency, especially for long trajectories with many segments.

contributions.claim: LATTE is a framework for adaptive segmentation in efficient and effective trajectory similarity learning.
LATTE uses lightweight road segment embeddings that decouple topological modeling from road segment feature modeling during training and decouple the complete embedding from inference.
LATTE adaptively merges consecutive trajectory segments into sub-trajectories and uses a tailored teacher-student knowledge distillation strategy for training.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present LATTE as a novel framework for learning adaptive segmentation for efficient and effective trajectory similarity learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: LATTE is evaluated against six state-of-the-art baselines using two real datasets.
The authors report that LATTE outperforms the best baselines by up to 34.6% in TSL effectiveness.
The authors report up to an 11.9× speedup in inference efficiency.

narrative_sequence.summary: TSL models encode variable-length trajectories as fixed-size vectors, and recent models use map-matched road networks for richer information.
Heavy modeling structures create overfitting and inefficiency, particularly for long trajectories.
LATTE combines lightweight decoupled road segment embeddings with learned adaptive segmentation.
A tailored knowledge distillation strategy trains a teacher first and then trains LATTE on adaptively segmented trajectories to retain representation capability at lower computational cost.
The authors report comparisons against six baselines on two real datasets, with gains in effectiveness and inference efficiency.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baseline names, evaluation protocols, or statistical significance of the reported results.
The abstract does not provide ablations, resource requirements, or details of the adaptive segmentation and distillation objectives.
